name: Arugula
tile_uses: The warm plate, tacos, toast, the salad
why_now: Arugula is a cool-weather green. In summer heat it bolts and turns harsh; planted in September, it's ready in October with a gentler, peppery bite. It's the first green in months that tastes like it wanted to grow.
how_to_choose: Small leaves are milder than big, deeply lobed ones
No wet or slimy leaves at the bottom of the bag or bunch
Bunches usually taste more of themselves than washed clamshells
buy_this_much: 2 bunches, or one big bag. It doesn't keep like the rest of the basket — use it first.
price_note: Bunches are often cheaper per ounce than clamshells.

flavor_paths.name: Raw, dressed last
flavor_paths.description: Olive oil, lemon, salt, right before eating. The default.

flavor_paths.name: As a topping
flavor_paths.description: A handful on anything warm, undressed. It wilts just enough.

flavor_paths.name: In the salad
flavor_paths.description: With pomegranate, dates, and feta. The weekend.

weekday_uses: On the warm plate over roasted squash and rice
In fish tacos in place of lettuce
On top of toast with ajvar and an egg
Beside a baked sweet potato, dressed with lemon
weekend_use: The base of the October salad: arugula, pomegranate, torn dates, and feta, dressed at the last second.
storage: Unwashed, wrapped in a dry paper towel inside a bag, in the crisper. Three or four days. Wash it right before using.
one_thing_to_learn: Dress greens at the last possible moment. Salt pulls water out of leaves, and oil weighs them down, so a salad dressed ten minutes early is a wilted salad. Put everything in the bowl, carry it to the table, and toss it there.
